text.title: django-pytest-mocking Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules for django-pytest-mocking: import-site patch, responses for HTTP, freezegun for time, Celery .delay() vs eager, plus the four spec-level branch rules the decision tree routes to per boundary kind.

rule.statement: Patch at the import site of the module under test, not at the definition site of the function being patched. If apps.payments.services imports stripe, patch "apps.payments.services.stripe", not "stripe.Charge.create". Always verify mock calls with assert_called_once_with or assert_called_once when the call is part of the contract. Use MagicMock for return values with attributes. Reset mocks between tests automatically (unittest.mock.patch as decorator does this).
rule.rationale: Python's import system binds names in each module separately. Patching at the definition site (stripe) does not affect the already-imported name in apps.payments.services.stripe. Patching at the import site replaces the name as seen by the code under test. assert_called_once_with verifies both that the call happened and that the arguments are correct — a critical part of the integration contract.

rule.statement: Use the responses library (pip install responses) to mock HTTP calls made via the requests library. Decorate the test or test class with @responses.activate to intercept calls. Add expected responses with responses.add() before calling the code under test. Assert on responses.calls to verify the request was made with the correct URL, method, and payload.
rule.rationale: responses intercepts at the transport level, so the production code uses the real requests library unchanged. Tests can verify the full request shape (URL, headers, body) and simulate various HTTP responses (200, 503, timeouts) without network access. This tests the integration contract without requiring a live server.

rule.statement: Use freezegun.freeze_time as a decorator or context manager to fix time in tests that use datetime.now(), timezone.now(), or datetime.date.today(). Pass an ISO datetime string to freeze_time. Use as a decorator for the entire test or as a context manager for part of the test (e.g., to simulate time passing mid-test). Prefer time-machine library (faster) over freezegun for new tests.
rule.rationale: Tests that compute relative times at run time are flaky: "coupon valid for 7 days from now" passes today but fails in the future. freeze_time makes the clock deterministic. Context-manager use enables "before/after expiry" scenarios in a single test. time-machine is a faster drop-in replacement if runtime is a concern.

rule.statement: Set CELERY_TASK_ALWAYS_EAGER=True in test settings to run Celery tasks synchronously. For tests that assert only that a task was enqueued (not that it ran), patch the task's delay method: @patch("apps.module.tasks.send_task.delay"). Assert with assert_called_once_with to verify the task was called with the correct arguments. Test the task function itself in a separate test class without mocking.
rule.rationale: CELERY_TASK_ALWAYS_EAGER makes integration tests simple: the task runs inline and you can assert on its side effects. But for service tests where you only want to verify "the service triggered the right task", patching delay is cleaner: it verifies the contract without actually executing the task's side effects.

rule.statement: When the boundary is an SDK or plain Python import (Stripe, Twilio, boto3, an internal client module), the boundaries[] entry MUST set technique="unittest-mock-patch" and a patch_target that starts with the consuming module's dotted path (apps.billing.services.stripe.Charge.create), never the library's own path (stripe.Charge.create); the validator rejects any patch_target whose prefix is not a module under apps/. When the boundary is a Django ORM call or a time.sleep inside a retry or rate-limit loop, no boundaries[] entry is written at all: the spec's anti_mocks MUST list "django-orm" and "time-sleep", the ORM case is tested with the db fixture plus factories, and the sleep case patches the retry decorator or rate-limiter object instead.

rationale.source: Python standard library documentation, unittest.mock 'Where to patch'; pytest-django documentation, db fixture

rule.rationale: unittest.mock replaces a name in one namespace, so patching stripe.Charge.create leaves the name apps.billing.services already bound to the real object and the test exercises production code while the mock records nothing. A mocked ORM proves only that the mock returned what the test told it to, and a no-op sleep lets a retry state machine that depends on elapsed time pass in CI and fail in production (fm-2 and fm-3); the anti_mocks list is what makes both refusals checkable instead of a convention that erodes.

rule.statement: When the boundary is an HTTP call made through the requests library, the boundaries[] entry MUST set technique="responses", patch_target to the full URL (scheme, host, path) the production code calls, and asserts that include at least one check on responses.calls (a len(responses.calls) count or a request.url / request.body match). The test MUST be decorated with @responses.activate and every expected URL registered with responses.add() before the code under test runs; a test that reaches the network fails, and a boundaries[] entry of this technique whose asserts check only the return value is rejected.
rule.rationale: responses intercepts at the requests transport adapter, so the production code path, headers, retries and JSON encoding are exercised unchanged and an unregistered URL raises ConnectionError instead of silently hitting a partner. Asserting on responses.calls is what distinguishes 'the service posted the webhook with this body' from 'the service returned something', which is the missing-call-assert antipattern in fm-5.

rule.statement: When the boundary is the clock (datetime.now(), timezone.now(), date.today(), or an expiry computed from them), the boundaries[] entry MUST set technique="freezegun" or "time-machine" with patch_target an ISO-8601 instant with an explicit UTC offset (2026-05-22T00:00:00Z), applied as a decorator on the test or a context manager around the time-sensitive block; the asserts MUST name the behaviour that flips at that instant (coupon.is_valid() is False). The code under test MUST read the clock at call time; any datetime.now() evaluated at module import or as a default argument is rejected, because no freezer can reach it.

rationale.source: freezegun documentation; time-machine documentation (Adam Johnson); Django documentation, django.utils.timezone.now

rule.rationale: A test that computes 'seven days from now' against the real clock passes on the day it is written and fails on a date nobody is watching; freezing the instant makes the expiry assertion deterministic and lets one test cover before and after the boundary with two context blocks. A default argument or module-level constant is evaluated once at import, before the freezer is installed, which is fm-4 and the reason the rule reaches into the production code, not only the test.

rule.statement: When the boundary is a Celery task, the boundaries[] entry MUST pick exactly one technique by test aim: "celery-eager" when the test asserts on the task's side effects (rows written, email in mail.outbox), which requires CELERY_TASK_ALWAYS_EAGER=True in the test settings and asserts on the effect, not on the task object; "celery-delay-patch" when the test asserts only that the service triggered the task, with patch_target the consumer's import path ending in .delay (apps.billing.services.send_invoice_task.delay) and asserts of assert_called_once_with on the task arguments. The same test MUST NOT do both, and the task body itself is tested in its own test class without either technique.

rationale.source: Celery documentation, 'task_always_eager' and 'Testing with Celery'; Python unittest.mock documentation

rule.rationale: Eager mode runs the task inline inside the caller's transaction, so a service test using it silently depends on the task's database writes and email sending, and a change inside the task breaks service tests that were never about it; patching .delay keeps the service test on its own contract, the arguments it enqueues. Mixing the two in one test either double-executes the side effect or asserts on a mock that eager mode bypassed, which is why the spec forces one technique per entry.
